This document contains the analysis scripts and report for the manuscript “A Course on AI for Pre-Service STEM and Language Teachers: A Quasi-Experimental Evaluation of Learning Outcomes Using Intelligent-TPACK and AI Literacy Instruments”. The R scripts, data are hosted at .

1 Methods

1.1 Participants

Code 
data_participants <- data %>%
  filter(time == "pre") %>%
  group_by(intervention, location, gender) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    n_complete = sum(complete.cases(.)),
    age_min = min(age, na.rm = T),
    age_max = max(age, na.rm = T),
    age_mean = mean(age, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    age_sd = sd(age, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    semester_min = min(semester, na.rm = T),
    semester_max = max(semester, na.rm = T),
    semester_mean = mean(semester, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    semester_sd = sd(semester, na.rm = T) %>% round(2)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
`summarise()` has grouped output by 'intervention', 'location'. You can
override using the `.groups` argument.

The study involved pre-service teachers from two universities of education in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. Participants were divided into a treatment group consisting of two intervention groups (STEM and language course), and a control group. Students in the treatment groups self-selected the courses “AI in STEM/Language Education” as part of their compulsory elective studies. The control group was recruited from other STEM courses at University 1 during the same semester.

In total, \(N=156\) students originally participated in the study (\(N_c=65\) in the control group, \(N_s= 53\) in the STEM course, and \(N_l=38\) in the language course), of which \(n=76\) completed both pre- and the posttest and were included in the analyses (\(n_c = 19\), \(n_s = 34\), \(n_l = 23\)).

Unfortunately, we observed a high drop-out rate between the pre- and posttest. We attribute this to several factors: First, the posttests were conducted in class close (one to two weeks) to the examination period, resulting in students not attending the in-person posttest sessions. For the control group, some lecturers executed the posttest during their teaching, while others did not. We suspect a high drop-out at the posttest for the control group due to both factors: students not attending the sessions close to the examination week and not conducting the tests at home or in their free study time.

Descriptive statistics of students’ demographics and pretest scores are presented in Table 1. The final sample size included in the analyses was \(n=76\), aged between \(20\) and \(41\) years (\(M=24.26\), \(SD=4.01\)), of which \(48\) identified as female and \(28\) as male. The students were enrolled in semester \(2\) to \(19\) (\(M=7.46\), \(SD=2.88\)). Of these, \(37\) students were at the Bachelor’s level and \(39\) at the Master’s level.

1.1.1 Effect Sizes for Group Differences for Covariates

Code 
vars_num <- c("age", "semester") # numeric outcomes
vars_cat <- c("gender", "students") # categorical outcomes

d <- data %>%
  filter(time == "pre") %>%
  mutate(
    gender = factor(gender, labels = c("Female", "Male")),
    students = factor(students, labels = c("Bachelor", "Master"))
  )

# eta^2 for numeric outcomes
eta_num <- purrr::map_dfr(vars_num, function(v) {
  f <- as.formula(paste(v, "~ intervention"))
  m <- lm(f, data = d)
  es <- effectsize::eta_squared(m, partial = TRUE)
  tibble(
    variable = v,
    effect = "eta2",
    value = es$Eta2[1],
    interpretation = effectsize::interpret_eta_squared(value) %>% as.character
  )
})
For one-way between subjects designs, partial eta squared is equivalent
  to eta squared. Returning eta squared.

  to eta squared. Returning eta squared.

# Cramér's V for categorical outcomes
cv_cat <- purrr::map_dfr(vars_cat, function(v) {
  tab <- table(d[[v]], d$intervention)
  cv <- effectsize::cramers_v(tab)
  tibble(
    variable = v,
    effect = "cramers_v",
    value = cv$Cramers_v,
    interpretation = effectsize::interpret_cramers_v(value) %>% as.character
  )
})

effectsizes_covariates <- bind_rows(eta_num, cv_cat) %>%
  mutate(
    value = apa_num(value)
  )

Code 
cohens_d_two_groups <- purrr::map_dfr(vars_num, function(v) {
  es <- effectsize::cohens_d(v, "treatment", d, pooled = TRUE)
  tibble(
    variable = v,
    effect = "cohens_d",
    value = es$Cohens_d,
    interpretation = effectsize::interpret_cohens_d(value) %>% as.character
  )
})

phi_two_groups <- purrr::map_dfr(vars_cat, function(v) {
  tab <- table(d[[v]], d$treatment)
  phi <- effectsize::phi(tab, adjust = F)
  tibble(
    variable = v,
    effect = "phi",
    value = phi$phi,
    interpretation = effectsize::interpret_phi(value) %>% as.character
  )
})

# combine
effectsizes_covariates__two_groups <- bind_rows(
  cohens_d_two_groups,
  phi_two_groups
) %>%
  mutate(
    value = apa_num(value)
  )

1.2 Materials

1.2.1 Translation Process

The Intelligent-TPACK, originally developed by Celik (2023), is widely used to assess teachers’ knowledge for pedagogical and ethical AI use based on the technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge (TPACK) framework. However, while some studies translate and use subsets of the Intelligent-TPACK (e.g., Mah & Groß, 2024), no empirically validated German translations of the full Intelligent-TPACK exists.

Therefore, for the Intelligent-TPACK by Celik (2023) as well as for items from the AI ethics subscale from Chiu et al. (2024), we translated the original items in a participative multi-step process involving not just experts from the fields of computer science and education, but also (pre-service) teachers. For this, we applied the Modified Direct Translation that includes translators and experts discussing the wording until reaching agreement (Behling & Law, 2025): First, seven researchers and experts in AI ED (additionally including one English teacher and one student teacher of Computer Science and English) translated the items independently. Second, we compared all translations and marked the items that received different translations. In a third step, we performed a group workshop with all translators in which the marked items were discussed and dot voting was applied to decide on the most apporopriate translation. Finally, three items that were still marked as questionable were discussed and further adapted with a native English teacher who teaches at University 2.

The translation and validation of the Intelligent-TPACK is reported in detail in Authors (in prep.).

1.3 Analysis

Note

Mixen wir manchmal treatment und intervention? Antwort Heiko: kann sein - sollte dann vereinheitlicht werden, bzw. wenn man es einführt, dann kann man auch sagen, dass treatment 3 conditions hat: STEM intervention, language intervention, control.

To examine the efficacy of the interventions, we conducted separate ANCOVA models for each outcome measure. In each model, posttest scores were regressed on treatment condition while controlling for the respective pretest score, gender, and semester count, consistent with our three-group pretest–posttest design.

Important

Derzeit fehlt die Erklärung für die Helmert-Contrast-Kodierung - ist das Absicht? Das muss ggf. nochmal angepasst werden - aber sonst weiß man nicht, woher der allgemeine Treatment effekt kommt:

We used a dummy-coded treatment variable using reversed Helmert contrasts to additionally contrast the differences between the control group and both intervention groups (“main treatment effect”).

Following the baseline equivalence criteria for randomized controlled trials proposed by the What Works Clearinghouse (Clearinghouse, 2022), we additionally considered baseline variables as covariates if group differences were statistically significant or if the standardized mean difference exceeded \(d = .05\). We tested for baseline differences between treatment groups in age, gender, semester count, and study level (Bachelor’s vs. Master’s). Statistically significant group differences were found for gender and semester count; therefore, these variables were included as covariates in all models (see Table 1).

That is, the final model for each outcome measure contained treatment, pretest score, gender, and semester count as fixed effects, and was specified as follows: lm_robust(outcome_post ~ treatment + outcome_pre + gender + semester ).

Posttest scores were standardized before running the analyses, so that the regression coefficients of the dummy variable indicating the respective treatment groups can directly be interpreted as Cohen’s \(d\) (Marsh et al., 2009).

Caution

Der folgende Satz steht bereits bei Statistical Software. Ggf. die Statistical Software dann direkt im Anschluss, oder sogar davor?

To compute heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC) standard errors, we used the lm_robust function from the estimatr package (Blair et al., 2025), specifying the HC3 estimator, as recommended for small samples (J. S. Long & Ervin, 2000).

The criterion of statistical significance was set at \(α=.05\).

The raw data and R scripts detailing the analyses can be accessed in the online supplement at .

1.3.1 Data Preparation and Cleaning

Code 
# get participants who only participated in pre or post test
data_dropouts <- data_all %>%
  group_by(code) %>%
  summarise(
    has_pre = any(time == "pre"),
    has_post = any(time == "post"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    n_pre_only = sum(has_pre & !has_post),
    n_post_only = sum(!has_pre & has_post),
    n_both = sum(has_pre & has_post)
  )

For data cleaning, we applied the following steps: First, we investigated which students, based on their pseudonyms, did not participate in both test sessions. Based on a string distance analysis using the Levenshtein distance (Levenshtein, 1966), we identified pseudonyms that were likely to belong to the same student but were entered slightly differently (e.g., due to typos or students who moved during the semester, as the address was part of their pseudonym). We then manually checked these pseudonyms and merged them if we believe they belonged to the same student. This resulted in \(n=24\) students being merged. We then removed students who only participated at the pretest (\(n=69\)) or only at the posttest (\(n=11\)). Further, some students conducted the post test twice. In this case, we only considered their first response in the analyses and dropped the second.

As for some self-constructed items students could choose “I don’t understand the item” as a response option, we recoded these responses as missing values (\(n=7\) responses to individual items).

For the Intelligent TPACK, AI ethics and perceived usefulness (sub)scales, we calculated the mean score across all items of the respective (sub)scale per student. For AI literacy, we calculated the sum score across all items. We additionally calculated the sum score for the subset of items of the AI literacy that directly reflect the topics addressed in the course, see SECTION MATERIALS.

1.3.2 Statistical Software

All analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2024). Data were prepared using dplyr (Wickham et al., 2023), tidyr (Wickham et al., 2024), and gtools (Warnes et al., 2023). Tables were created with arsenal (Heinzen et al., 2021), vtable (Huntington-Klein, 2023), modelsummary (Arel-Bundock, 2022), and kableExtra (Zhu, 2024). Figures were produced using ggplot2 (Wickham, 2016), ggsci (Xiao, 2024), and jtools (J. A. Long, 2022). The ANCOVA models were estimated using lm_robust from the estimatr package (Blair et al., 2025). To compute heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC) standard errors, we specified the HC3 estimator, as recommended for small samples (J. S. Long & Ervin, 2000). Where applicable, pairwise comparisons were obtained with emmeans (Lenth, 2025).

2 Results

Descriptive statistics of students’ pretest scores are presented in Table 1. As expected, students attending the STEM course and students from the control group, which was recruited from pre-service STEM teachers, reported significantly higher ratings in all Intelligent TPACK subscales compared to students attending language course, which predominantly consisted of students not studying a STEM subject as their second subject. We didn’t find significant differences between the intervention groups for AI literacy, AI ethics, and perceived usefulness at the pretest.

The descriptive statistics for students’ outcome measures at pretest and posttest by treatment group are shown in the top half of Figure 1, Figure 2, and Figure 3. At the bottom half of these figures, the ANCOVA-adjusted predicted posttest scores are displayed, with predictions standardized to a common pretest value and adjusted for gender and semester count.

For all outcome measures, we first report the main effect of treatment condition (i.e., the difference between the control group and the intervention groups) on posttest scores after adjusting for pretest scores, gender, and semester count. We then report the planned contrasts comparing the control group with the intervention groups and, subsequently, the contrast between the two intervention groups (STEM vs. language course).

Code 
# reshape data to wide format for ancova
data_wide <- data %>%
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(
      code,
      intervention,
      group,
      gender,
      semester,
      students,
      location
    ),
    names_from = time,
    values_from = all_of(outcomes)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # scale the posttest score so that the estimates are approximations of Cohen's d
    across(all_of(outcomes %>% paste0("_post")), scale),

    treatment = factor(ifelse(
      intervention == "control",
      "control",
      "intervention"
    ))
  )

data_wide_unscaled <- data %>%
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(
      code,
      intervention,
      group,
      gender,
      semester,
      students,
      location
    ),

    values_from = all_of(outcomes)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    treatment = factor(ifelse(
      intervention == "control",
      "control",
      "intervention"
    ))
  )

colnames(contrasts.treatment) <- c("-c+t")

2.1.1 AI Literacy – Full Scale

Note

Am Anfang von Results schreiben wir, dass wir immer erst den Main-Effekt berichten und dann erst alle Kontraste. Wenn wir immer Main-Effekt und dann die zwei Interventions vergleichen, dann sollten wir das oben auch so schreiben.

Important

überprüft, ob es medium oder moderate efffect heißt

Note

Bezeichnung gesamte AI literacy scale: full vs. complete vs whole vs entire vs. “with all XY items”

Tip

Ich würde die Berichtserstattung der Skalen möglichst einheitlich machen: * showed significantly greater improvement vs. showed significantly higher posttest scores * with a medium-sized effect vs. indicating a medium-sized effect etc.

For the full AI literacy scale, students in the intervention groups did not show significantly greater improvement than students in the control group, \(\beta\) = 0.28, SE = 0.27, t(70) = 1.04, p = .301. The two intervention groups also did not differ significantly from each other, \(\beta\) = -0.42, SE = 0.24, t(70) = -1.74, p = .086, although the estimate suggests a small-to-moderate advantage for the STEM group.

Looking at the post-hoc contrasts, the contrast between the control and STEM groups was marginally significant, \(\beta\) = -0.49, SE = 0.28, t(70) = -1.78, p = .079, indicating a small-to-moderate effect in favor of the STEM group. Similarly, the STEM group tended to score higher than the language group with a small-to-moderate effect size, \(\beta\) = 0.42, SE = 0.24, t(70) = 1.74, p = .086.

Note

Brauchen wir den nächsten Satz?

However, as can be seen in Figure 1, students in all conditions showed descriptively higher AI literacy at posttest, with the strongest increase observed among pre-service STEM teachers.

2.1.2 AI Literacy – Study-Specific Subset

Note

statt die Effektstärke ans Ende zu setzen, könnte man auch folgendes schreiben:

students in the intervention groups showed significantly greater improvements with a medium-sized effect, \(\beta\) = 0.61, SE = 0.23, t(70) = 2.69, p = .009, compared to students in the control group.

oder

we found significantly differences between the control and the intervention groups, with a medium-sized effect in favor of the intervention groups, \(\beta\) = 0.61, SE = 0.23, t(70) = 2.69, p = .009.

For the study-specific subset of the AI literacy items, students in the intervention groups showed significantly greater improvements in their knowledge than students in the control group, \(\beta\) = 0.61, SE = 0.23, t(70) = 2.69, p = .009, indicating a medium-sized effect in favor of the intervention groups. In addition, the two intervention groups differed significantly, \(\beta\) = -0.67, SE = 0.28, t(70) = -2.41, p = .019, with the estimate indicating a medium-sized advantage for the STEM group.

Note

Ersten Satz verstehe ich nicht: geht es hier um die Post-Test-Scores oder Improvement? Das steht da nicht.

Ggf. showed descriptivle higher improvement in study-specific AI literacy scores than students in the control group, and this difference was statistically significant with a medium-sized effect, \(\beta\) = 0.61, SE = 0.23, t(70) = 2.69, p = .009.

Auch beim zweiten Satz: entweder “scored higher after intervention than …” oder “showed significantly greater improvement the control group, with a medium-sized effect, \(\beta\) = -0.67, SE = 0.28, t(70) = -2.41, p = .019.”

As can be seen in Figure 1, students in both intervention groups showed descriptively higher AI literacy scores than students in the control group. Post-hoc contrasts showed that students in the STEM course scored significantly higher on the study-specific AI literacy subset than students in the control group, \(\beta\) = -0.95, SE = 0.26, t(70) = -3.58, p < .001, indicating a large effect in favor of the STEM group, whereas the difference between students in the language course and the control group was not statistically significant, \(\beta\) = -0.28, SE = 0.27, t(70) = -1.04, p = .303.

2.2 Intelligent TPACK and AI Ethics

The descriptive results of students’ ratings of perceived knowledge in Intelligent TPACK and AI ethics as well as the ANCOVA-adjusted predicted posttest ratings are shown in Figure 2, and Table 3 lists the results of the ANCOVA.s As can be seen in Figure 2, all pre-service teachers reported their intelligent TPACK knowledge to be around or below the middle of the scale at the pretest, while the intervention groups reported, on average, values significantly higher than the middle value of the scale at the posttest.

Across all subscales related to Intelligent TPACK, namely Intelligent TK, Intelligent TPK, Intelligent TCK, Intelligent TPACK, and AI ethics, students in the intervention groups reported significantly greater improvements than students in the control group with large effect sizes ranging from 0.89 to 1.30. These effects were reflected in significantly higher pretest-adjusted posttest ratings for both intervention groups compared with the control group. The two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, with the exception of the Intelligent TCK subscale, for which students in the STEM group reported significantly greater improvement than students in the language group, see Table 3.

2.2.1 Intelligent TK

For Intelligent TK, students in the intervention groups reported significantly greater improvement than students in the control group, \(\beta\) = 1.08, SE = 0.34, t(70) = 3.20, p = .002, indicating a large positive effect in favor of the intervention groups. The two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, \(\beta\) = -0.17, SE = 0.20, t(70) = -0.83, p = .408.

2.2.2 Intelligent TPK

Tip

Ich würde nicht wechseln zwischen marginal significant, tends to oder approaches signifiance. Lieber bei einem bleiben.

The difference between the two intervention groups was only marginal significant, \(\beta\) = -0.49, SE = 0.28, t(70) = -1.77, p = .081, with a small-to-moderate effect size in favor of the language group.

For Intelligent TPK, students in the intervention groups reported significantly greater improvement than students in the control group, \(\beta\) = 1.01, SE = 0.31, t(70) = 3.25, p = .002, indicating a large positive effect in favor of the intervention groups. The two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, although the effect approached significance, \(\beta\) = -0.49, SE = 0.28, t(70) = -1.77, p = .081, suggesting a small-to-moderate advantage for the language STEM group.

2.2.3 Intelligent TCK

For Intelligent TCK, students in the intervention groups reported significantly greater improvement than students in the control group, \(\beta\) = 0.91, SE = 0.29, t(70) = 3.08, p = .003, indicating a large positive effect in favor of the intervention groups. Notably, this was the only subscale for which the two intervention groups also differed significantly, \(\beta\) = -0.58, SE = 0.23, t(70) = -2.51, p = .014, with the estimate indicating a medium-sized advantage for the STEM group.

2.2.4 Intelligent TPACK Core

For the Intelligent TPACK core subscale, students in the intervention groups reported significantly greater improvement than students in the control group, \(\beta\) = 1.30, SE = 0.27, t(70) = 4.79, p < .001, indicating a large positive effect in favor of the intervention groups. The two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, \(\beta\) = -0.33, SE = 0.22, t(70) = -1.53, p = .130.

2.2.5 Intelligent TPACK (GenAI)

For Intelligent TPACK related to GenAI, students in the intervention groups reported significantly greater improvement than students in the control group, \(\beta\) = 0.89, SE = 0.29, t(70) = 3.09, p = .003, indicating a large positive effect in favor of the intervention groups. The two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, although the effect approached significance, \(\beta\) = -0.45, SE = 0.25, t(70) = -1.77, p = .081, suggesting a small-to-moderate advantage for the language group.

2.2.6 AI Ethics

For AI ethics, students in the intervention groups reported significantly greater improvement than students in the control group, \(\beta\) = 1.31, SE = 0.29, t(70) = 4.46, p < .001, indicating a large positive effect in favor of the intervention groups. The two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, \(\beta\) = -0.05, SE = 0.24, t(70) = -0.21, p = .836.

```{r rerun-models-with-proper-contrasts}
data_wtf <- data %>%
  droplevels %>%
  mutate(
    location = factor(
      location,
      levels = c("PH Schwäbisch Gmünd", "PH Ludwigsburg")
    ),
    treatment = factor(ifelse(
      intervention == "control",
      "control",
      "intervention"
    ))
  )

## define contrast Control vs Exp1+Exp2 - vermutlich bessere version, da die Estimates "stimmen"
mat <- cbind(
  c(1 / 3, 1 / 3, 1 / 3), # Durchschnitt aller 3 Gruppen
  c(-1, .5, .5), # Vergleich Control vs Mittel der beiden Interventions-Gruppen
  c(0, -1, 1)
) # Vergleich Sprache vs MINT
contrasts.CvsExp <- solve(t(mat))[, -1]
colnames(contrasts.CvsExp) <- c("-c+STEM_language", "-STEM+language")
contrasts(data_wtf$intervention) <- contrasts.CvsExp

# GENDER
# female: -1/2
# male : +1/2
contrasts.gender <- cbind(c(-1 / 2, 1 / 2))
colnames(contrasts.gender) <- c("-m+f")
contrasts(data_wtf$gender) <- contrasts.gender

# LOCATION
# SG UE: -1/2
# L UE: +1/2
contrasts.location <- cbind(c(-1 / 2, 1 / 2))
colnames(contrasts.location) <- c("-SGUE+LUE")
contrasts(data_wtf$location) <- contrasts.location

# TIME
# pre: -1/2
# post: +1/2
contrasts.time <- cbind(c(-1 / 2, 1 / 2))
colnames(contrasts.time) <- c("-pre+post")
contrasts(data_wtf$time) <- contrasts.time

data <- data_wtf
# refit all lmer_prepost_all with new data
lmers_prepost_all <- lapply(
  outcomes,
  fit_lmer,
  groups,
  time,
  controls,
  random_terms_lmer,
  NULL,
  data = data
)
names(lmers_prepost_all) <- outcomes
```

# Methods

## Participants

```{r data_participants}
data_participants <- data %>%
  filter(time == "pre") %>%
  group_by(intervention, location, gender) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    n_complete = sum(complete.cases(.)),
    age_min = min(age, na.rm = T),
    age_max = max(age, na.rm = T),
    age_mean = mean(age, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    age_sd = sd(age, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    semester_min = min(semester, na.rm = T),
    semester_max = max(semester, na.rm = T),
    semester_mean = mean(semester, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    semester_sd = sd(semester, na.rm = T) %>% round(2)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```


The study involved pre-service teachers from two universities of education in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. Participants were divided into a **treatment group** consisting of two intervention groups (STEM and language course), and a **control group**.
Students in the treatment groups self-selected the courses "AI in STEM/Language Education" as part of their compulsory elective studies. The control group was recruited from other STEM courses at University 1 during the same semester. 

In total, $N=`r length(unique(data_all$code))`$ students originally participated in the study ($N_c=`r data_all %>% filter(intervention == "control") %>% distinct(code) %>% nrow()`$ in the control group, $N_s= `r data_all %>% filter(intervention == "stem") %>% distinct(code) %>% nrow() `$ in the STEM course, and $N_l=`r data_all %>% filter(intervention == "language") %>% distinct(code) %>% nrow() `$ in the language course), of which $n=`r data_participants$n %>% sum`$ completed both pre- and the posttest and were included in the analyses ($n_c = `r data_participants%>%filter(intervention=="control") %>% select(n)%>%sum`$, $n_s = `r data_participants%>%filter(intervention=="stem") %>% select(n)%>%sum`$, $n_l = `r data_participants%>%filter(intervention=="language") %>% select(n) %>% sum`$).

Unfortunately, we observed a high drop-out rate between the pre- and posttest. We attribute this to several factors: First, the posttests were conducted in class close  (one to two weeks) to the examination period, resulting in students not attending the in-person posttest sessions. For the control group, some lecturers executed the posttest during their teaching, while others did not. We suspect a high drop-out at the posttest for the control group due to both factors: students not attending the sessions close to the examination week and not conducting the tests at home or in their free study time.

Descriptive statistics of students' demographics and pretest scores are presented in [@tbl-participants]. The final sample size included in the analyses was $n=`r data_participants$n %>% sum`$, aged between $`r data_pre$age %>% min`$ and $`r data_pre$age %>% max`$ years ($M=`r data_pre$age %>% mean %>% round(2)`$, $SD=`r data_pre$age %>% sd %>% round(2)`$), of which $`r data_pre %>% filter(gender=="Weiblich")%>%nrow`$ identified as female and $`r data_pre%>%filter(gender=="Männlich")%>%nrow`$ as male.
The students were enrolled in semester $`r data_pre$semester %>% min`$ to $`r data_pre$semester %>% max`$ ($M=`r data_pre$semester %>% mean %>% round(2)`$, $SD=`r data_pre$semester%>%sd%>%round(2)`$). Of these, $`r data_pre%>%filter(students=="bachelor") %>% nrow`$ students were at the Bachelor's level and $`r data_pre%>%filter(students=="master")%>%nrow`$ at the Master's level.


```{r table-participants, result = "asis"}
#| label: tbl-participants
#| tbl-cap: "Demographic Data of the Three Experimental Groups."
# render as table
format <- ifelse(
  knitr::is_html_output(),
  "markdown",
  ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "latex", "markdown")
)

var_names <- list(
  gender = "Gender",
  age = "Age",
  semester = "Semester Number",
  students = "Study Level",
  isp = "Completed Integrated Semester Internship",
  subject1 = "Subject 1",
  subject2 = "Subject 2",
  studies = "Study Program",
  location = "University",
  TK = "Intelligent TK",
  TCK = "Intelligent TCK",
  TPK = "Intelligent TPK",
  TPACK_total = "Intelligent TPACK",
  AILIT = "AI Literacy",
  PU = "Perceived Usefulness",
  Ethics = "AI Ethics"
)

kable(
  summary(
    tableby(
      intervention ~
        location +
        age +
        gender +
        semester +
        students +
        TK +
        TCK +
        TPK +
        TPACK_total +
        Ethics +
        AILIT +
        PU,
      data %>%
        filter(time == "pre") %>%
        mutate(
          gender = factor(gender, labels = c("Female", "Male")),
          students = factor(students, labels = c("Bachelor", "Master"))
        ) %>%
        droplevels(),
      cat.test = "chisq",
      chisq.correct = T,
      control = tableby.control(test = T, total = T, digits = 2)
    ),
    labelTranslations = var_names,
    pfootnote = T,
    text = F
  ),
  escape = T,
  format = format,
  booktabs = T
)
```

### Effect Sizes for Group Differences for Covariates
```{r group-differences-effectsizes}
vars_num <- c("age", "semester") # numeric outcomes
vars_cat <- c("gender", "students") # categorical outcomes

d <- data %>%
  filter(time == "pre") %>%
  mutate(
    gender = factor(gender, labels = c("Female", "Male")),
    students = factor(students, labels = c("Bachelor", "Master"))
  )

# eta^2 for numeric outcomes
eta_num <- purrr::map_dfr(vars_num, function(v) {
  f <- as.formula(paste(v, "~ intervention"))
  m <- lm(f, data = d)
  es <- effectsize::eta_squared(m, partial = TRUE)
  tibble(
    variable = v,
    effect = "eta2",
    value = es$Eta2[1],
    interpretation = effectsize::interpret_eta_squared(value) %>% as.character
  )
})

# Cramér's V for categorical outcomes
cv_cat <- purrr::map_dfr(vars_cat, function(v) {
  tab <- table(d[[v]], d$intervention)
  cv <- effectsize::cramers_v(tab)
  tibble(
    variable = v,
    effect = "cramers_v",
    value = cv$Cramers_v,
    interpretation = effectsize::interpret_cramers_v(value) %>% as.character
  )
})

effectsizes_covariates <- bind_rows(eta_num, cv_cat) %>%
  mutate(
    value = apa_num(value)
  )
effectsizes_covariates %>% kable

cohens_d_two_groups <- purrr::map_dfr(vars_num, function(v) {
  es <- effectsize::cohens_d(v, "treatment", d, pooled = TRUE)
  tibble(
    variable = v,
    effect = "cohens_d",
    value = es$Cohens_d,
    interpretation = effectsize::interpret_cohens_d(value) %>% as.character
  )
})

phi_two_groups <- purrr::map_dfr(vars_cat, function(v) {
  tab <- table(d[[v]], d$treatment)
  phi <- effectsize::phi(tab, adjust = F)
  tibble(
    variable = v,
    effect = "phi",
    value = phi$phi,
    interpretation = effectsize::interpret_phi(value) %>% as.character
  )
})

# combine
effectsizes_covariates__two_groups <- bind_rows(
  cohens_d_two_groups,
  phi_two_groups
) %>%
  mutate(
    value = apa_num(value)
  )
```

## Materials

### Translation Process
The Intelligent-TPACK, originally developed by @celik2023, is widely used to assess teachers’ knowledge for pedagogical and ethical AI use based on the technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge (TPACK) framework.
However, while some studies translate and use subsets of the Intelligent-TPACK [e.g., @mah.gross2024], no empirically validated German translations of the full Intelligent-TPACK exists. 

Therefore, for the Intelligent-TPACK by @celik2023 as well as for items from the AI ethics subscale from @chiu.ahmad.ea2024, we translated the original items in a participative multi-step process involving not just experts from the fields of computer science and education, but also (pre-service) teachers.
For this, we applied the *Modified Direct Translation* that includes translators and experts discussing the wording until reaching agreement [@behling.law2025]: First, seven researchers and experts in AI ED (additionally including one English teacher and one student teacher of Computer Science and English) translated the items independently. Second, we compared all translations and marked the items that received different translations. In a third step, we performed a group workshop with all translators in which the marked items were discussed and dot voting was applied to decide on the most apporopriate translation. Finally, three items that were still marked as questionable were discussed and further adapted with a native English teacher who teaches at University 2.

The translation and validation of the Intelligent-TPACK is reported in detail in @authorsinprep.

## Analysis 
::: {.callout-note}

Mixen wir manchmal treatment und intervention?
Antwort Heiko: kann sein - sollte dann vereinheitlicht werden, bzw. wenn man es einführt, dann kann man auch sagen, dass treatment 3 conditions hat: STEM intervention, language intervention, control. 

:::

To examine the efficacy of the interventions, we conducted separate ANCOVA models for each outcome measure. In each model, posttest scores were regressed on treatment condition while controlling for the respective pretest score, gender, and semester count, consistent with our three-group pretest–posttest design.

::: {.callout-important}
>Derzeit fehlt die Erklärung für die Helmert-Contrast-Kodierung - ist das Absicht?
Das muss ggf. nochmal angepasst werden - aber sonst weiß man nicht, woher der allgemeine Treatment effekt kommt:

We used a dummy-coded treatment variable using reversed Helmert contrasts to additionally contrast the differences between the control group and both intervention groups ("main treatment effect").
:::



Following the baseline equivalence criteria for randomized controlled trials proposed by the What Works Clearinghouse [@WWC2022], we additionally considered baseline variables as covariates if group differences were statistically significant or if the standardized mean difference exceeded $d = .05$. We tested for baseline differences between treatment groups in age, gender, semester count, and study level (Bachelor’s vs. Master’s). Statistically significant group differences were found for gender and semester count; therefore, these variables were included as covariates in all models (see [@tbl-participants]).

That is, the final model for each outcome measure contained treatment, pretest score, gender, and semester count as fixed effects, and was specified as follows:
`lm_robust(outcome_post ~ treatment + outcome_pre + gender + semester )`.




Posttest scores were standardized before running the analyses, so that the regression coefficients of the dummy variable indicating the respective treatment groups can directly be interpreted as Cohen's $d$ [@marsh2009].


::: {.callout-caution}
Der folgende Satz steht bereits bei Statistical Software.
Ggf. die Statistical Software dann direkt im Anschluss, oder sogar davor?
:::

To compute heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC) standard errors, we used the *lm_robust* function from the *estimatr* package [@blair2025], specifying the HC3 estimator, as recommended for small samples [@long2000].

The criterion of statistical significance was set at $α=.05$.

The raw data and *R* scripts detailing the analyses can be accessed in the online supplement at <OSF>.


### Data Preparation and Cleaning

```{r}
# get participants who only participated in pre or post test
data_dropouts <- data_all %>%
  group_by(code) %>%
  summarise(
    has_pre = any(time == "pre"),
    has_post = any(time == "post"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    n_pre_only = sum(has_pre & !has_post),
    n_post_only = sum(!has_pre & has_post),
    n_both = sum(has_pre & has_post)
  )
```

For data cleaning, we applied the following steps: First, we investigated which students, based on their pseudonyms, did not participate in both test sessions. Based on a string distance analysis using the Levenshtein distance [@levenshtein1966], we identified pseudonyms that were likely to belong to the same student but were entered slightly differently (e.g., due to typos or students who moved during the semester, as the address was part of their pseudonym). We then manually checked these pseudonyms and merged them if we believe they belonged to the same student. This resulted in $n=24$ students being merged.
We then removed students who only participated at the pretest ($n=`r data_dropouts$n_pre_only`$) or only at the posttest ($n=`r data_dropouts$n_post_only`$).
Further, some students conducted the post test twice. In this case, we only considered their first response in the analyses and dropped the second.

As for some self-constructed items students could choose "I don't understand the item" as a response option, we recoded these responses as missing values ($n=`r data %>%
  select(all_of(c(list_items_i_tpack, list_items_pu)%>%unlist)) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) %>% sum`$ responses to individual items).

For the Intelligent TPACK, AI ethics and perceived usefulness (sub)scales, we calculated the mean score across all items of the respective (sub)scale per student. For AI literacy, we calculated the sum score across all items. We additionally calculated the sum score for the subset of items of the AI literacy that directly reflect the topics addressed in the course, see SECTION MATERIALS.

### Statistical Software
All analyses were conducted in *R* [@R2024]. Data were prepared using *dplyr* [@wickham2023:dplyr], *tidyr* [@wickham2024], and *gtools* [@warnes2023]. Tables were created with *arsenal* [@heinzen2021], *vtable* [@huntington2023], *modelsummary* [@arel-bundock2022], and *kableExtra* [@zhu2024]. Figures were produced using *ggplot2* [@wickham2016], *ggsci* [@xiao2024], and *jtools* [@long2022]. The ANCOVA models were estimated using *lm_robust* from the *estimatr* package [@blair2025]. To compute heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC) standard errors, we specified the HC3 estimator, as recommended for small samples [@long2000]. Where applicable, pairwise comparisons were obtained with *emmeans* [@lenth2025].

All analyses were conducted in *R* [@R2024]. The ANCOVA models were estimated using *lm_robust* from the *estimatr* package [@blair2025]. To compute heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC) standard errors, we specified the HC3 estimator, as recommended for small samples [@long2000]. Where applicable, pairwise comparisons were obtained with *emmeans* [@lenth2025].

# Results
Descriptive statistics of students' pretest scores are presented in [@tbl-participants].
As expected, students attending the STEM course and students from the control group, which was recruited from pre-service STEM teachers, reported significantly higher ratings in all Intelligent TPACK subscales compared to students attending language course, which predominantly consisted of students not studying a STEM subject as their second subject. We didn't find significant differences between the intervention groups for AI literacy, AI ethics, and perceived usefulness at the pretest.

The descriptive statistics for students’ outcome measures at pretest and posttest by treatment group are shown in the top half of [@fig-ai-lit], [@fig-tpack], and [@fig-pu]. At the bottom half of these figures, the ANCOVA-adjusted predicted posttest scores are displayed, with predictions standardized to a common pretest value and adjusted for gender and semester count.

For all outcome measures, we first report the main effect of treatment condition (i.e., the difference between the control group and the intervention groups) on posttest scores after adjusting for pretest scores, gender, and semester count. We then report the planned contrasts comparing the control group with the intervention groups and, subsequently, the contrast between the two intervention groups (STEM vs. language course).

::: {.callout-note}

Man könnte jetzt hier auch sagen (da bei ANCOVA der Change dasselbe ergibt):

> on students' change in the respective outcome measures from pretest to posttest, after adjusting for pretest ...

:::

```{r compute-ancovas}
# reshape data to wide format for ancova
data_wide <- data %>%
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(
      code,
      intervention,
      group,
      gender,
      semester,
      students,
      location
    ),
    names_from = time,
    values_from = all_of(outcomes)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # scale the posttest score so that the estimates are approximations of Cohen's d
    across(all_of(outcomes %>% paste0("_post")), scale),

    treatment = factor(ifelse(
      intervention == "control",
      "control",
      "intervention"
    ))
  )

data_wide_unscaled <- data %>%
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(
      code,
      intervention,
      group,
      gender,
      semester,
      students,
      location
    ),
    names_from = time,
    values_from = all_of(outcomes)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    treatment = factor(ifelse(
      intervention == "control",
      "control",
      "intervention"
    ))
  )

contrasts.treatment <- cbind(c(-1 / 2, 1 / 2))
colnames(contrasts.treatment) <- c("-c+t")
contrasts(data_wide$treatment) <- contrasts.treatment

ancovas <- lapply(
  outcomes,
  fit_ancova,
  groups,
  # we remove University as a covariate as we only have control students at University 2
  setdiff(controls, "location"),
  "HC3",
  data_wide
)
names(ancovas) <- outcomes
tc2 <- nrow(summary(ancovas[[1]])$coefficients)
tc1 <- tc2 - 1

ancovas_unscaled <- lapply(
  outcomes,
  fit_ancova,
  groups,
  # we remove University as a covariate as we only have control students at University 2
  setdiff(controls, "location"),
  "HC3",
  data_wide_unscaled
)
names(ancovas_unscaled) <- outcomes

ancovas_two_groups <- lapply(
  outcomes,
  fit_ancova,
  "treatment",
  setdiff(controls, "location"),
  "HC3",
  data_wide
)
names(ancovas_two_groups) <- outcomes
```

## Intelligent TPACK and AI Ethics
The descriptive results of students' ratings of perceived knowledge in Intelligent TPACK and AI ethics as well as the ANCOVA-adjusted predicted posttest ratings are shown in [@fig-tpack], and [@tbl-ancova-tpack-summary] lists the results of the ANCOVA.s As can be seen in [@fig-tpack], all pre-service teachers reported their intelligent TPACK knowledge to be around or below the middle of the scale at the pretest, while the intervention groups reported, on average, values significantly higher than the middle value of the scale at the posttest.

Across all subscales related to Intelligent TPACK, namely Intelligent TK, Intelligent TPK, Intelligent TCK, Intelligent TPACK, and AI ethics, students in the intervention groups reported significantly greater improvements than students in the control group <mark>with large effect sizes ranging from 0.89 to 1.30</mark>. ~~These effects were reflected in significantly higher pretest-adjusted posttest ratings for both intervention groups compared with the control group.~~ The two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, with the exception of the Intelligent TCK subscale, for which students in the STEM group reported significantly greater improvement than students in the language group, see [@tbl-ancova-tpack-summary].

### Intelligent TPACK (GenAI)
For Intelligent TPACK related to GenAI, students in the intervention groups reported significantly greater improvement than students in the control group, `r report_beta(ancovas[["TPACKgenai"]], "intervention-c+STEM_language")`, indicating a large positive effect in favor of the intervention groups. The two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, although the effect approached significance, `r report_beta(ancovas[["TPACKgenai"]], "intervention-STEM+language")`, suggesting a small-to-moderate advantage for the language group.

### AI Ethics
For AI ethics, students in the intervention groups reported significantly greater improvement than students in the control group, `r report_beta(ancovas[["Ethics"]], "intervention-c+STEM_language")`, indicating a large positive effect in favor of the intervention groups. The two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, `r report_beta(ancovas[["Ethics"]], "intervention-STEM+language")`.


## Perceived Usefulness
Descriptive results of pre-service teacher students' perceived usefulness of AI in their teaching as well as the ANCOVA-adjusted posttest ratings are listed in [@fig-pu], while the results of the ANCOVA analysis for perceived usefulness are presented in [@tbl-ancova-pu-summary].

```{r fig-pu, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Descriptive Statistics of Students' Perceived Usefulness Ratings Over Time by Treatment Group.", out.width="100%",fig.width=7, fig.height=6.5}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
outcomes_pu <- c("PU", "PU1", "PU2", "PU3", "PU4")
# Define outcome scale labels
pu_labels <- c(
  PU = "Full Scale",
  PU1 = "PU1: \nIncreases \nTeaching Quality",
  PU2 = "PU2: \nReduces Workload",
  PU3 = "PU3: \nIncreases \nEffectiveness",
  PU4 = "PU4: \nUsefulness for Work"
)

# Prepare data: compute predictions + reshape to long format
data_pu_long_individual <- prepare_comparison_data(
  data_wide_unscaled,
  outcomes_pu,
  pu_labels,
  ancovas_unscaled
)

# Get sample size
n_pu <- data_long %>%
  filter(outcome %in% outcomes_pu) %>%
  filter(!is.na(score)) %>%
  summarise(n = n_distinct(code)) %>%
  pull(n)

# Raw data plot
p_pu_raw <- plot_facet_outcome(
  data_long %>% filter(str_detect(outcome, "^(PU)")),
  ncol = 5,
  outcome_labels = pu_labels,
  y_title = "Rating",
  y_zoom = c(3.3, 4.8),
  show_legend = FALSE,
  show_strip_labels = TRUE,
  plot_title = "Perceived Usefulness",
  plot_subtitle = paste0("N = ", n_pu),

  # show_n_per_facet = TRUE
)

# Predicted adjusted data plot
p_pu_pred <- plot_facet_outcome(
  data_pu_long_individual,
  ncol = 6,
  outcome_labels = NULL, # Hide labels in row 2
  y_title = "ANCOVA adj. rating",
  y_zoom = c(3.3, 4.8),
  show_legend = TRUE,
  show_strip_labels = FALSE,
  plot_title = NULL,
  plot_subtitle = NULL,
  error_bars = FALSE
  # show_n_per_facet = TRUE
)

# Combine and display
combine_raw_pred_plots(p_pu_raw, p_pu_pred)
```

::: {.callout-note}

Ich spreche bei der PU nicht von "improvement" weil ich finde das passend nicht. Kann man es so formulieren wie ich es gerade habe?

**Antwort Heiko**: statt improvement könnte man auch einfach change sagen, aber so wie du es gerade formuliert hast, finde ich es auch gut.

> did not report a significantly greater change in their perceived usefulness of AI than students in the control group, `r report_beta(ancovas[["PU"]], "intervention-c+STEM_language")`.

Ich würde aber bei perceived usefulness noch ergänzen, welche es konkret ist. Dann holt man den Leser mehr ab:
> Regarding the overall perceived usefulness of AI in their teaching, ...
:::

For overall perceived usefulness, we did not find a significant treatment effect on students’ perceived usefulness ratings. Students in the intervention groups did not differ significantly from students in the control group in their pretest-adjusted posttest ratings, `r report_beta(ancovas[["PU"]], "intervention-c+STEM_language")`. The two intervention groups also did not differ significantly from each other, `r report_beta(ancovas[["PU"]], "intervention-STEM+language")`. For an overview of the ANCOVA results, see [@tbl-ancova-pu-summary].

```{r  pu - contrasts}
pu_between_contrasts <- lapply(
  ancovas[grepl("^(PU)", names(ancovas))],
  function(m) {
    emmeans(m, ~intervention) %>%
      contrast(interaction = "pairwise", adjust = "none")
  }
)
if (!is_word) {
  print(pu_between_contrasts)
}
```

When investigating the individual items of the perceived usefulness scale, we did not find any significant differences between the control and intervention groups for any of the items. For item PU3, we observed a tendency toward a medium-sized effect between the intervention groups, `r report_contrast_beta(pu_between_contrasts[[4]], 3)`, with higher values in the STEM group than in the language group. For the same comparison on item PU4, we found a significant difference, `r report_contrast_beta(pu_between_contrasts[[5]], 3)`, again indicating a medium-sized effect in favor of the STEM group.
